opus-5.5.text:
I think the big unresolved challenge is integration in a way that's actually meaningful, not just technically possible. With a cancer patient you've got so many different streams of information: imaging like CT and MRI, pathology slides, genomic and molecular profiling, lab values over time, treatment history, clinical notes, and increasingly things patients report themselves. Each of those was collected for a different purpose, at different times, at different resolutions, and often in different institutions with different standards.

So the first problem is just that the data don't line up neatly. A CT scan is a dense, high-dimensional snapshot of the whole tumor. A biopsy samples a tiny piece of it. Genomics might come from that one biopsy, or from blood. The clinical record is a messy, irregular time series. And for any given patient a lot of it is missing, and it's not missing at random. Sicker patients get more tests, certain centers order certain assays, and that missingness carries information that can fool a model if you're not careful.

The second problem is scale versus dimensionality. Each modality on its own can have thousands or millions of features, but the number of patients with all of those modalities, plus good outcome data, is often in the hundreds. That's a recipe for overfitting, and it's why you see a lot of beautiful results that don't hold up when you take them to another hospital.

Then there's the question of what the model is actually learning. In my own work on things like radiomics, we're trying to pull quantitative signals from imaging that reflect underlying tumor biology. The hope is that imaging becomes a non-invasive window into what's happening at the molecular level, and that's exactly where multimodal approaches should shine. But proving the model is capturing biology, rather than scanner differences or site-specific quirks, is really hard.

And finally, even if you solve all of that, you have to make it useful to a clinician. A combined risk score that nobody can interpret, or that doesn't change a treatment decision, isn't going to help patients. So for me the unresolved piece is building integration methods that are robust across institutions, honest about missing data, interpretable enough to trust, and tied to a real clinical question. That requires data sharing, and also close collaboration between people who build models and people who treat patients.

r001.rationale: The response says each modality can have thousands or millions of features while patients with complete data and outcomes may number only in the hundreds, creating a risk of overfitting.

r002.rationale: It describes overfitting from the feature-to-patient imbalance, but does not state that using AI does not overcome limits in statistical power.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that we still don't know how to integrate these data types in a way that's actually faithful to the biology and useful in the clinic at the same time.

When a patient comes through a cancer centre, we collect an enormous amount: CT and MRI images, pathology slides, genomic and transcriptomic profiles, lab values, the free text in clinical notes, and then outcomes that unfold over months or years. Each of those modalities lives at a different scale, is captured at a different time point, and has its own noise and missingness. Imaging is a snapshot of the whole tumour and its environment. Sequencing often comes from a tiny biopsy that may not represent the whole lesion. Notes are written by busy clinicians with their own shorthand. So the first unresolved piece is simply alignment. What does it mean to say this voxel, this gene expression value, and this sentence in a note are describing the same thing?

The second piece is that most multimodal methods assume you have everything for everyone, and in real patients you almost never do. People get scanned at outside hospitals, sequencing isn't ordered, a biopsy fails. If a model only works on the complete cases, it ends up being trained on a biased, often healthier or better-resourced subset, and it quietly stops being applicable to the patients who might benefit most. Handling missing modalities gracefully, rather than imputing them away or dropping the patient, is still very much open.

Third, and this is the one I think about most, is whether fusion actually buys us something beyond the best single modality. It's easy to concatenate features and report a small bump in AUC. It's much harder to show that the imaging is contributing something the genomics didn't already tell you, and to make that interpretable to an oncologist who has to act on it. We need evaluation frameworks that ask what each modality adds, when, and for whom, instead of just whether the number went up.

And underlying all of it is the practical reality of how the data is governed. The imaging sits in PACS, the genomics sits in a research database, the notes sit in the EHR, and each has its own privacy constraints and custodians. A lot of the integration problem is as much institutional as it is algorithmic. If I had to name the one challenge that ties it together, it's building models that respect the structure and the gaps in how this data is actually generated, rather than pretending we have a clean, complete, perfectly aligned dataset. We're not there yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes many data modalities, gaps, and alignment challenges, but does not identify having more measured variables than patients or overfitting from that imbalance.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that AI remains constrained by statistical power.

astra-6.text:
I think the unresolved challenge is how we bring all of those different types of data together in a way that actually helps us understand the patient. We might have imaging, pathology, genomic information, and clinical records, but they describe different aspects of the disease, at different scales and at different points in time. And we don’t necessarily have every type of data for every patient.

So it’s more than simply putting everything into one model. How do we learn from those complementary sources, handle what’s missing, and show that combining them gives us something useful beyond any one source alone? Ultimately, we want that richer picture to help guide decisions for an individual patient.

r001.rationale: The response names several data types and notes that some may be missing, but it does not identify having many measured variables relative to the number of patients as a source of overfitting.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that AI remains constrained by statistical power.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the unresolved challenge is how we bring those different types of data together in a way that actually helps us understand the patient. We might have medical images, pathology, genomic information, and a clinical history, but they describe different aspects of the disease at very different scales. And we don’t necessarily have all of those data for every patient.

So how do we build models that can learn from that complexity, handle what’s missing, and give us information that’s useful for a treatment decision? It’s more than putting everything into one big model. We need to understand what each source contributes and whether combining them helps us make better predictions for patients we haven’t seen before.

r001.rationale: It mentions diverse data types and incomplete data, but does not identify having many measured variables relative to few patients as an overfitting problem.

r002.rationale: It discusses building models that handle complexity and missing data, but does not state that AI remains constrained by statistical power.
